Mullai Systems: What Does the Canvas Actually Say?

A product team in Coimbatore has a careful map of its customers' pain. It is no longer sure the map is of the customer who pays.

Discovery & Design · Solution Design & Prototyping · Case 40

1. Sunday night, Coimbatore

On the evening of Sunday, 18 October 2026, Yazhini Gopalakrishnan sat on the floor of her flat in Coimbatore with three printed exhibits in front of her and a fourth she had not printed. Tiruppur would shut for Dussehra on Tuesday, and the factories Mullai Systems sold to would be dark for nine days.

The call was at 7.30 the next evening, India time: 6.00 pm for Masira Retail Group's observer in Dubai, 4.00 pm for Yashna Gokaraju in Berlin, 10.00 am for Yashwin Gundimeda in Toronto and Yogendra Gattamaneni in New Jersey, 10.00 pm for Yuktha Ghantasala in Singapore. Yazhini, who ran product, was to present one slide: What our customers are actually buying.

She had written and deleted it four times. Eighteen months earlier Mullai had run the most careful research the company had attempted: 148 conversations with garment exporters, coded and argued over. Out of it came a customer profile — jobs, pains, gains — and a value map of what Mullai would build. The product worked. Yet the module exporters' owners said they would pay for was the one almost nobody opened.

She could not decide whether the research was wrong, the product was wrong, or her canvas had mapped relievers onto one person's pains while another signed the cheque.

2. Mullai Systems, 2019 to 2026

Mullai was founded in March 2019 by Yoganand Garimella, eleven years a merchandiser for a Bengaluru knitwear exporter, and Yashas Gurumurthy, a Pune engineer who had never stood on a factory floor. Their first product replaced a spreadsheet for lab-dip approvals, and sold slowly and well.

The decision that still shapes everything came in September 2021. Masira Retail Group, a Dubai fashion and home-textiles group, asked Mullai to build its vendor portal for roughly 190 Indian and Bangladeshi suppliers. The contract was worth ₹3.6 crore over eighteen months to a company then burning ₹9 lakh a month. Mullai signed it, and signed clause 11.4 with it.

Clause 11.4 gave Masira's suppliers free access for the life of the agreement — which is why seven of today's sixty-three accounts pay nothing, and twenty-seven more were sold at a pilot price set to look defensible beside "free". It also gave Masira a right of review over any module that "generates, stores or presents evidence capable of use in a commercial claim or dispute between a buyer and a supplier". In 2021 it read as boilerplate about inspection photographs; in 2026 it describes the thing exporters say they want.

Mugil Capital Partners led a ₹22 crore Series A in March 2024 on the strength of the Masira relationship and a plan to sell the portal directly to exporters. Mullai now has 39 people: 14 in Bengaluru, 11 in Pune, 7 in Coimbatore, two in Singapore, two in New Jersey, and one each in Berlin, Toronto and Dubai. Figure 1 sets out the sequence.

Figure 1. Axis linear in time: 1 January 2019 at x = 90, one year = 120 px, one month = 10 px; each marker sits at the first of its named month. The dashed marker is a covenant date.

3. The industry

Tiruppur is the densest knitwear cluster in India, selling into a buyer market that has hardened for five years. Trade-body statements put its knitwear exports in the region of ₹28,000 crore a year. Against Bangladesh and Vietnam the advantage is speed and small runs, not price, so pre-production is where orders are won and margin lost.

Four forces bear on the product. European Union and United Kingdom buyers now demand traceability a WhatsApp thread cannot produce. GST e-invoicing, e-BRC realisation, RoDTEP claims and ICEGATE filings generate paperwork clerks redo more than anyone admits. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 matters because the claim-defence module photographs packing tables, and packing tables have workers at them. And the incumbents are not software companies: Excel, WhatsApp and the merchandiser's memory. Zoho and Freshworks have made Indian firms comfortable paying for software; neither sells a tech-pack workflow.

Masira in Dubai and Morgenlicht Mode GmbH in Düsseldorf are buyers, not exporters: they pay more and on time, and their interests are not the factories'.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Between March and July 2025, Yazhini and Yashna ran 148 interviews across 61 exporters in Tiruppur, Bengaluru and Ludhiana. In May they added a card-sort: each respondent named up to three pains from a deck of nine. Added mid-stream, it reached only 96 of the 148, and every share in Exhibit 1 is of those 96.

The profile froze in July 2025. Sample round-trip time was the top pain, named by 71 of 96 respondents, or 74.0 per cent; scattered buyer comments came second and claim deductions third. Mullai built against that ranking to January 2026; Exhibit 2 is the value map, Figure 2 its sketch.

The first paying account went live in February 2026; by 30 September there were 63. Exhibit 2 was unambiguous: the modules built against the top-ranked pains were used weekly by most accounts, while the claim-defence file — third-ranked pain, second-costliest module — was written in weekly by only 9 of 63 accounts, which is 14.3 per cent.

In August 2026 Yuvasri Gnanasekaran's team asked 41 owners what discovery never had: if you paid for one module, which, and how much? Sixteen chose the claim-defence file at a median of ₹18,000 a month, double the next (Exhibit 3).

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. The first is the respondent mix: of the 96 card-sorts, 41 came from merchandising managers and only 22 from owners. Sample round-trip time was named by 35 of the 41 merchandisers, or 85.4 per cent, and by 6 of the 22 owners, which is 27.3 per cent. Claim deductions ran the other way: 18 of 22 owners, or 81.8 per cent, against 9 of 41 merchandisers, or 22.0 per cent. Mullai built against the merchandiser's ranking, and the merchandiser does not sign the invoice.

The second is that the gains column was never filled from data: the guide after May carried no gain prompts. Relievers were mapped onto measured pains; gain creators were written from conviction, and there is no exhibit for them because there is nothing to put in one.

The third is arithmetic, and it is in the board pack already circulated. The deck's CAC payback of 13.1 months spreads ₹96 lakh of sales and marketing spend across all 63 live accounts and recovers it at list price. Both bases are wrong: only 56 accounts pay anything, and the realised average is ₹10,259 a month, not ₹14,000. Exhibit 4 works it through to about 21.7 months; the deck is unchanged.

5. The people

Yazhini Gopalakrishnan, 38, vice-president, product, Coimbatore. Position: the canvas is not wrong, only incomplete — relievers were mapped to the user's pains, none to the buyer's. Incentive: her credibility is the discovery. Not saying: she knew in June 2025 that owners were under-represented and let it go.

Yoganand Garimella, 46, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: sell what owners will pay for; settle clause 11.4 commercially. Incentive: the ₹2 crore ARR gate. Not saying: Masira's buying director has hinted at renewal at a lower fee, and the board does not know.

Yashas Gurumurthy, 41, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. Position: the file is built, so this is adoption, not architecture, and a rebuild is five months Mullai cannot fund. Incentive: six of his twenty-five engineers are ring-fenced to Masira's uptime SLA. Not saying: photo capture was never tested on packing-hall 4G.

Yuvasri Gnanasekaran, 35, head of sales, India, Tiruppur. Position: price the claim-defence file at ₹18,000 and the pipeline doubles by Pongal. Incentive: quota is signed accounts, not retained ones. Not saying: 29 of her 41 owners were introductions she chose.

Yashna Gokaraju, 33, design lead, Berlin. Position: redraw the canvas as three profiles — merchandiser, owner, buyer's inspector. Incentive: she proposed this in June 2025 and was overruled. Not saying: her fully loaded €78,000 is about ₹78 lakh at finance's ₹100-to-the-euro rate, against ₹91 lakh for the seven-person Coimbatore team — ₹13 lakh each.

Yashwin Gundimeda, 31, data scientist, Toronto. Position: neither Exhibit 3 nor Exhibit 5 carries the weight put on it. Incentive: he has nothing to lose by saying so. Not saying: he has been interviewing since August.

Yuktha Ghantasala, 36, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: usage, not stated preference, is the honest signal, and it says the sample tracker is the product. Incentive: 19 of the 27 pilot accounts renew by March 2027. Not saying: four of the nineteen will not renew at list price.

Yogendra Gattamaneni, 52, head of sales, North America, Edison, New Jersey. Position: forget exporters — one Masira is worth sixty factories. Incentive: his pipeline is buyer-side. Not saying: two exploratory calls with Morgenlicht, which Yoganand does not know about.

7. Voices

"Every owner I meet talks about claims. Every single one. Put ₹18,000 on the module and let me sell."

8. The options as Yazhini sees them

A. Price on the sample tracker. Make F1 and F3 the paid core at a price the usage in Exhibit 6 defends, and leave F5 in the bundle. No engineering, no Masira exposure. It also prices the module whose median in Exhibit 3 was ₹6,500, the lowest but one.

B. Rebuild around the claim-defence file. Fix the upload path, ship a deduction-reconciliation view, price at ₹18,000. Yashas puts it at five months on nineteen engineers, and it needs a clause 11.4 submission before Mullai can sell a tool to contest a buyer's deduction — and Masira is 60.4 per cent of revenue.

C. Unbundle. Sell F1 at ₹6,500, F2 at ₹9,000 and F5 at ₹18,000 separately and let the market sort the canvas out. It triples the sales motion for a team adding seven accounts a month.

D. Go to the buyer side. Sell the portal to buying groups: Yogendra puts one Masira at sixty factories on revenue, and has two conversations open. Perhaps eight such groups buy Indian knitwear at scale, and exporters become a channel.

Each option takes the canvas as given and argues which column to bet on; Yazhini suspects that is the error. All four price a pain reliever; none is built on a measured gain, because none was measured. All four treat "the exporter" as one customer, where Exhibit 1 shows four job roles with opposed rankings. And B's reliever may relieve nothing: the pain of a deduction is not the absence of photographs, it is a buyer who has already decided.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is on Monday, 19 October 2026. Mullai held ₹4.90 crore of cash on 30 September 2026 and has been burning ₹46 lakh a month net; from 1 October that is about 10.7 months, to the third week of August 2027. The Series A terms require ₹2 crore of annual recurring revenue by 31 March 2027, counting subscription revenue only: Masira's platform fee is excluded. Run rate today is ₹68.94 lakh, so the gap is ₹131.06 lakh; at ₹10,259 a month per paying account, or ₹1,23,108 a year, ₹131.06 lakh ÷ ₹1.23108 lakh = 106.5, so 107 further paying accounts in six months — eighteen a month, against seven a month over the last eight months.

Masira's agreement comes up for renewal on 31 December 2026, and clause 11.4 survives it. Six of twenty-five engineers are committed to the Masira SLA. The Act's obligations on the claim-defence file — consent, purpose limitation, retention — are scoped but unbuilt. Hiring is frozen but for one offer to a Tiruppur implementation lead at ₹18 lakh. And Tiruppur shuts for Dussehra from Tuesday, costing Yuvasri nine selling days.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reconstruct Mullai's canvas from Exhibits 1 and 2. Which modules relieve a measured pain, and on whose ranking?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 point in opposite directions. What would have to be true for each to be the better guide to what Mullai builds?
  3. Exhibit 5 underwrites the market-size claim in the pack. List what it cannot establish, and what evidence would.
  4. The gain creators were never grounded in data. Design the smallest prototype-and-critique cycle that would test one against one customer profile, with its decision rule stated first.
  5. Clause 11.4 was signed in 2021 to fund a company burning ₹9 lakh a month. Was it a mistake then, and does it constrain the answer now?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October 2026. What does Yazhini do before the call, what slide does she put up, and what does she tell a board holding a payback of 13.1 months?

At a quarter past eleven she squared the exhibits and put them face down, drew two columns and a line between them on the back of Exhibit 3, then stopped: she could not decide which of the three belonged on the right-hand side.

Lokavi Stores: Mapping Relief to Pain

A decision case on the Value Proposition Canvas

1. Opening

At 7.40 on the evening of Tuesday, 3 November 2026, Vasantha Eluri sat alone on the second floor of Lokavi Stores' office in Adyar, Chennai, with three printed pages and a cold filter coffee. Diwali was five days away, on Sunday. The shops her company served were stacking cartons of oil, sugar and sweets.

Vasantha was Head of Product. By Friday, 6 November, she had to tell the chief executive, Vikas Emani, how to spend an ₹80 lakh build budget for the next quarter. The squads would start on Monday, 9 November. Three proposals sat on her desk, and each could be defended.

2. Company background

Lokavi Stores was founded in 2022 and sells Lokavi Dukaan, a phone app that helps neighbourhood grocery shops, the kiranas, keep their customers' credit ledgers and send payment reminders over WhatsApp. It competes for the same shopkeepers as Khatabook and OkCredit, and sits in a market where Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart are pulling the evening basket toward ten-minute delivery, while ONDC and Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner court the same counters with their own offers.

By 31 October 2026, 38,000 shops had registered and 14,200 were active that month, meaning they had made at least one ledger entry; the other 23,800 had registered and drifted away. The active base split across Chennai (5,400), Coimbatore (3,100) and Hyderabad (5,700). A fifth of them, 2,840 shops, paid ₹199 a month, an annualised ₹67.8 lakh. Lokavi's founders had built the product on one belief: that a shopkeeper's main trouble was remembering who owed what.

3. The situation

That belief had been drawn onto a Value Proposition Canvas in January, and Vasantha had insisted on redrawing it in September. The right-hand side listed what Lokavi offered; the left listed what shopkeepers were trying to do, what hurt, and what would delight them. Redrawing meant going back to the shops. Between 21 September and 16 October, Vinaya Edara's research team in Hyderabad interviewed 120 shopkeepers drawn from September's active base, stratified as 45 in Chennai, 30 in Coimbatore and 45 in Hyderabad. Each was handed six pain cards and asked to choose the three that hurt most.

Exhibit 1 shows the result. Every shopkeeper chose exactly three, so the table holds 360 mentions. The pain named most often, by 88 of the 120, was not recovering udhaar from customers. It was being unable to buy stock on credit from a distributor when cash ran short. Udhaar recovery, the pain Lokavi was built to relieve, came second, with 79.

4. The people

Vikas Emani, co-founder and chief executive in Chennai, wants a story for the next funding round. He prefers whatever moves revenue fastest. Vinaya Edara, who leads customer research from Hyderabad, trusts what she heard in the shops and wants the top pain addressed, but fears building before anyone has shown the demand is real. Vignesh Ellur, the data scientist in Toronto, distrusts any claim that the pilot shops resemble the rest; he works ten and a half hours behind Chennai and sends his notes overnight. Valli Edupuganti, an investor director in Singapore, has asked a single question: which proposal can Lokavi prove worked by March?

5. The pilot and the options

One piece of evidence cut across the debate. From 14 September to 11 October, Lokavi had tested supplier credit in Coimbatore with a grocery distributor and a Chennai non-banking finance company, which would bear the credit risk under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules. The distributor had nominated 60 shops; 42 placed at least one order on 14-day credit, which is 70.0 per cent of the 60 offered. Together they placed 96 orders worth ₹36.48 lakh, an average of ₹38,000. By 2 November, 39 of the 42 had repaid every order on time, 92.9 per cent. Lokavi earned a 1.2 per cent fee on order value, ₹43,776 in all, or ₹1,042 for each of the 42 shops over the four weeks.

Vignesh was quick to point out the limit: the distributor chose its own favoured customers, and four weeks cannot show how shops behave in a lean season. Three courses were open, summarised in Exhibit 3 and drawn against the calendar in Figure 1.

Option A: deepen the reminders. Add Tamil, Telugu and Hindi voice reminders for ₹28 lakh, ready by Monday, 21 December. It is safe and quick, but it improves a pain already rated strong.

Option B: build supplier credit. Spend ₹64 lakh on credit ordering with the distributor and finance partner, ready by Monday, 11 January, in time for Pongal on Thursday, 14 January 2027. It addresses the top pain with the pilot behind it. The finance partner's pricing lapses on Monday, 30 November, so this option fits the partner's clock.

Option C: test first. Spend ₹9 lakh on a hand-run test with 150 shops chosen by Lokavi, not by a distributor, in all three cities, closing on Friday, 11 December. Build only if at least 53 of the 150 order, which is 35 per cent, and 90 per cent of those repay on time, judged on orders placed up to 27 November so every order falls due by 11 December. A build would then run 14 December to 15 February, missing Pongal and requiring a fresh quote from the partner.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which jobs, pains and gains sit on the customer side of Lokavi's canvas, and which does the current product relieve?
  2. Why do 80 per cent use of the reminders and 5 per cent use of the festival planner each mislead if read alone? What does Exhibit 2 not tell Vasantha?
  3. What can the Coimbatore pilot support, and what can it not? Would you accept a 70.0 per cent take-up as evidence for all 14,200 shops?
  4. Which option would you fund on Friday, and what decision rule would you attach to it?

7. A note for the learner

The Value Proposition Canvas asks one question of every feature: which named pain does it relieve, and which gain does it create? The test is a match between the two sides, not the quality of either. Lokavi's reminders are well made and well used, and they relieve the second pain. The first pain had nothing aimed at it; the planner targeted a cause (poor planning) that shopkeepers did not recognise, so it relieved no ranked pain. A good answer notices that usage shows a feature is liked, not that the biggest pain is gone.

One defensible path is Option B, with a stated stop rule. The reasoning: Option A spends ₹28 lakh improving a pain on which 83.5 per cent of the 79 affected shops said reminders helped a lot. Option B addresses the 88 mentions, and the pilot shows real behaviour, not opinion: 70.0 per cent ordered and 92.9 per cent of those repaid on time. Option C is the most disciplined test, but it gives up Pongal, a major stocking season, and it risks the partner's terms. The pilot's weakness, hand-picked shops, can be answered inside B. Release the first version to shops Lokavi selects itself, using the same bar as Option C: release the remaining funds only if at least 35 per cent of offered shops order and 90 per cent repay on time.

This is not the only sound answer. A student who picks Option C should explain why a missed Pongal is cheaper than building on a biased pilot. What the canvas settles is narrower and firmer: Option A should not win on the ground that it relieves a pain.
exp20v2-sol.vpc:
Value Proposition Canvas

Does the solution actually relieve the pains and create the gains the research found?

1. A Tuesday in Pune

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Amruta Bokil, head of product at Ekdhara Fresh, was given until the board meeting of 9 October to defend a number. Ekdhara buys fruit and vegetables from the Pune market yard at Gultekdi and delivers to about 340 neighbourhood grocery stores. Its founder, Avinash Badami, had proposed ₹180 lakh for the next two quarters: ₹120 lakh to build Enroot, an ordering app in which a store owner places tomorrow's order the previous evening, and ₹60 lakh as a float to extend credit. The app was Bokil's project. The credit float was Badami's idea and had never been tested.

The evidence was mixed. Between July and August, Bokil's team had interviewed 24 store owners in Hadapsar, Kothrud and Pimpri. From 24 August to 2 September, 11 of them had used a stripped-down Enroot for ten days. Ananth Bagade, who ran operations from Hyderabad, reported that the pilot stores reordered happily. Asha Bhalla, who owns a store in Hadapsar and had been in the pilot, said something more careful: "I like not going to the market at four in the morning. But I still pay cash on delivery, and my cash is what I am short of."

Badami wanted a yes or no. Bokil had a feeling that Bhalla had named the gap, but a feeling is not an argument, and ₹180 lakh was most of a year's product budget. She needed a way to show, line by line, which of the things owners had said hurt were relieved by what the team had built, and which were not. That tool is the Value Proposition Canvas.

2. The idea

The Value Proposition Canvas is a two-sided worksheet. One side is a customer profile for a single customer segment: the jobs the customer is trying to get done, the pains (bad outcomes, obstacles and risks that stand in the way of those jobs) and the gains (outcomes the customer wants or would welcome). The other side is a value map of the offering: the products and services, the pain relievers (specific things that remove or reduce a named pain) and the gain creators (specific things that produce a named gain). Fit is the degree to which relievers and creators match the pains and gains that matter most.

Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur introduced the Business Model Canvas in 2010. Its value proposition box was a single sticky note, and teams filled it with slogans. Osterwalder, Pigneur, Gregory Bernarda and Alan Smith unpacked that box in Value Proposition Design (2014), drawing on jobs-to-be-done thinking, which holds that customers "hire" products to make progress in a situation. The canvas was invented to stop a team from describing its offering in its own terms and to force every claim of value to be tied to something the customer said.

The sentence Bokil could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "Every feature we are paying for must point at a pain or a gain a named segment told us about, and we should be able to say how much of it the customer felt relieved."

3. How it works

The method has five steps, and the order matters because the customer side must be finished before the product side is judged. First, fix a single segment: here, owner-operated grocery stores in Pune that sell fresh produce and buy it daily. Second, list jobs, pains and gains, in the customer's words, from interviews or observation. Third, rank them. Bokil asked each of the 24 owners to name the three pains that bothered them most, and counted how many owners put each one in their top three. Gains were collected the same way: each owner also named their top three gains. Every owner therefore gave 3 picks per side, 72 per side in all. Picks that fell outside the five listed pains or five listed gains were recorded as "other" (3 of the 72 pain picks and 8 of the 72 gain picks). Because an unlisted item has no reliever to rate, the weights and maxima below count listed items only. That is a convention, and the next section shows it matters.

Fourth, and this is the step practitioners usually leave implicit, record how each pain relief or gain creator performed in the customer's hands, not in the team's head. Bokil asked the 11 pilot owners to say, for each item, whether Enroot relieved it "not at all", "somewhat", "mostly" or "fully", and scored those answers 0, 1, 2 and 3 using the most common answer. Fifth, combine importance and relief into a fit score, and compare it with a decision rule written down before the arithmetic is done. Without that last piece the score is a mood.

The score used here is simple. For each item, points equal the number of owners who ranked it (its weight) times the relief rating. The maximum is three times the weight. Fit is the sum of points over the sum of maxima. Nothing in this arithmetic is sophisticated, which is the point: a reader can recompute it and argue with each input.

4. A worked example, line by line

Figure 2 and the tables below carry Ekdhara's numbers. Weights are counts out of all 24 interviewed owners. The pilot distributions are out of the 11 pilot owners; the eleven answers per row are listed in the order not at all / somewhat / mostly / fully. Credit, a pain and a gain, was not part of version 1, so it scores 0 by construction. One caution before the tables: the weights come from 24 interviewed owners, the ratings from 11 owners who chose to join the pilot, and nothing shows that the 11 are representative of the 24.

Bokil's rule, written on 3 September, after the pilot ended on 2 September but before she totalled anything, was to build only if the combined fit reached 65 per cent (on listed items) and none of the top-three pains was rated below 2. Version 1 failed both tests, and failed the second badly, because the third-ranked pain scored zero. The listed-items convention flatters the score, and the page should say so. Had the 11 unlisted picks (3 + 8) been counted with zero relief, each side's maximum would rise: 3 × (72 + 72) = 432. Had credit been rated only "somewhat" (1), the points would be 119 + 14 = 133 and 107 + 13 = 120, a combined 253 of 399, or 63.4 per cent, below the threshold and failing the top-three rule. 5. Nuances worth knowing

Fit is claimed for one segment, not for "the market"

A canvas is only meaningful for one profile. The 24 owners were all produce-heavy stores in Pune; a supermarket chain or a restaurant buyer would have a different list. Blend segments and the ranking becomes an average that describes nobody.

Pains and gains are not mirror images

A pain is something that obstructs the job; a gain is an outcome that would be welcome. Relieving "spoilage" does not by itself create "fresh stock". Customers often name both for the same underlying need, as owners did for credit, and a team that counts both can quietly double-weight it. Credit accounts for 14 + 13 = 27 of the 133 weight units (69 + 64), about 20 per cent. If it is counted once, by dropping the credit gain, version 1 scores 226 of 360 (62.8 per cent) and version 2 scores 254 of 360 (70.6 per cent). The ranking of the two versions survives; the gap shrinks from 13.5 points to 7.8. A rule that says "65 per cent" is fragile near that edge, which is why the top-three condition matters as well.

Stated importance is not revealed importance

Owners were asked what bothered them. What they actually do with their time and money may differ. Owners rank the 4 a.m. trip as a pain, yet it is plausible that some value it because they negotiate there. Counting mentions is a first approximation; observed behaviour is a better one.

A reliever is an outcome, not a feature

"Photo at delivery" is a feature; "I no longer argue about short weight" is a reliever. The test is whether the customer, using the thing, reports less of the pain. Nine of the 11 pilot owners said the photo helped only "not at all" or "somewhat", which is why a feature the engineers were proud of rated 1.

Fit is not demand, and fit is not a business

The book distinguishes problem-solution fit (the canvas), product-market fit (people actually buy and return) and business-model fit (it makes money at scale). A 70 per cent canvas score is the first of these. It says nothing about willingness to pay or about default risk on the credit float.

The canvas cannot show what was not found

It maps the pains the team heard. If the 24 owners never mentioned that their landlords dislike pre-dawn deliveries, the tool will not either. It also ignores alternatives: the owner who relieves the cash pain by borrowing from the wholesaler next door is not on the page.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small, large

Ekdhara is a hybrid. The store owner is both buyer and user, which keeps the canvas simple, but the store owner's own customers shape what counts as a gain, as the "farm fresh" item shows. A marketplace version of Enroot, where farmers sold to stores directly, would need a second canvas for farmers, whose pains (payment delays, rejected loads) would pull against the stores' wish for lower prices. In a large company the same tool succeeds only when ratings are collected from customers by someone other than the team being rated.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is the commonest. Ekdhara's early value map listed "AI-based demand forecasting", which sounded impressive and answered nothing any owner had said; it was struck out after Bokil asked which sentence it served. The second is more damaging: before the pilot, the team had rated the price lock a 3 itself; owners rated it 2, and the credit gap would not have shown if the team had graded alone. The cheapest diagnostic in both cases takes minutes, which is exactly why teams skip it.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Bokil's decision looks like this. The segment is named. The pains and gains come with counts and the denominator beside them, so a reader can see that 19 means 19 of 24. The decision rule is written before the arithmetic, and its date relative to the evidence is disclosed. Relief ratings come from customers and carry their distributions, so that "mostly" is shown to mean 6 of 11 and not a consensus. Every unrelieved top-three item is a visible row of zeros, not a footnote. The canvas ends with the single cheapest experiment that would move the uncertain input, and a threshold for it, not with a recommendation to "explore further".

9. What Bokil decided

She did not ask for the ₹180 lakh. She asked for ₹1.65 lakh: a three-week credit pilot, from 14 September to 4 October, with the same 11 stores, a cap of ₹15,000 per store (11 × ₹15,000 = ₹1,65,000) and settlement in seven days. The rule, agreed with Badami in advance: if at least 7 of the 11 owners rate credit "mostly" or "fully", and fewer than two stores are late on payment, the board is asked on 9 October to release the ₹120 lakh build and the ₹60 lakh float. Otherwise the money stays where it is and the team goes back to the owners. Two cautions apply. First, the scoring in section 4 uses the most common answer, while this gate counts owners answering "mostly" or "fully"; they are different tests, and a split such as 2 / 3 / 4 / 2 has a most common answer of "mostly" yet only 6 of 11 at "mostly" or above. The gate decides; the 70.2 per cent figure only shows what a modal rating of 2 would imply. Second, with seven-day settlement, a draw made after 27 September falls due after the pilot ends on 4 October, and a draw after 2 October falls due after the board meets on 9 October. The lateness test can therefore be judged only on part of the draws, and Bokil planned to say so to the board. Her reasoning was that the canvas had shown version 1 could not pass, and that the cheapest way to learn whether version 2 could was to test the one rating that decided it.

What to learn next: the value proposition statement, which turns a validated fit into one sentence a customer would recognise, and which is only as good as the canvas behind it. Study it after this, because writing the statement first tends to hide gaps that the canvas exposes.

Two questions to sit with. If Bhalla's own words had been the only evidence, which row of the table would have been left blank, and what in your own work resembles that row? And in the canvas you would build next week, who rates the relief, and how would you know that they are not you?

Discovery & Design › Solution Design & Prototyping

The Value Proposition Canvas

Does the solution actually relieve the pains and create the gains that discovery found — and can anyone show the arithmetic?

1. Two companies, two live decisions

On 11 March 2026, in Nashik, Bhavya Chemburkar rebuilt a one-page exhibit. Chemburkar ran product at Elaan Labworks, which sells software to multi-site pathology-laboratory chains. Its platform, Esvara, came out of nine months of discovery: 74 chains contacted, 52 willing to talk, 43 inside the segment. The pricing committee met on 27 March under a rule the founders never waived: ship nothing unless verified annual relief to a reference customer is three times the price. Chemburkar's exhibit said 4.28 times. A version from six weeks earlier, by a manager who divided one prevalence figure by the wrong denominator, said 2.62 times.

On 3 February 2026, eleven hundred kilometres south, Bhaumik Chonkar had the opposite problem: large numbers and no adoption. Chonkar's Elanta Mobility, in Coimbatore, sold Esadhan, a retrofit telematics dongle with battery-health and charge-scheduling software, to electric three-wheeler fleets. On a reference fleet of 320 vehicles it cut idle days from 11.4 per cent of revenue days to 7.0 per cent: an operator gain of ₹18.51 lakh a year against a price of ₹4.64 lakh. Four operators had signed. In three, after ninety days, the schedule was being followed on fewer than one day in five, and Bhupen Chawathe, the hardware lead, suspected unplugging. The proposition was true, the buyer had signed it, and the value was not arriving.

Both decisions turn on one question: whether what is built lands on what was found. This page argues that the canvas is far more demanding than its format suggests, that almost every serious failure around it is a failure of denominators and incidence, and that its quantitative treatment is where the field's real disagreements live.

2. The idea, its history, its disputes

The canvas is two halves that must correspond. On the right is the customer profile: the jobs a customer in a specific role is trying to get done, the pains that attend them, the gains wanted. On the left is the value map: products and services, pain relievers addressing named pains, gain creators producing named gains. A canvas is not a description of a product but a claim that a reliever addresses a particular ranked pain of a particular customer, and it is useful exactly to the extent that the claim can be falsified.

The lineage explains the blind spots. Value proposition enters business language through a 1988 McKinsey paper by Michael Lanning and Edward Michaels: a proposition is a choice quantified against alternatives. In 2006 James Anderson, James Narus and Wouter van Rossum sorted propositions into all-benefits, favourable points of difference and resonating focus, allowing only the third the name. Anthony Ulwick's outcome-driven innovation supplied the apparatus: customers are unreliable about solutions and reliable about outcomes, which can be scored. Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur formalised the business model canvas in 2010 and, in 2014 with Gregory Bernarda and Alan Smith, zoomed into one block to produce the canvas now taught.

Six schools have a stake in it and do not agree. The differences show only at the level of specific propositions.

Exhibit 1 — What each school would and would not sign
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Canonical canvas (Osterwalder, Pigneur) “Fit is correspondence, re-achieved; relievers name ranked pains.” “The canvas tells you which pains matter.”
Outcome-driven innovation (Ulwick) “Score importance and satisfaction on outcome statements.” “Put pains and gains in separate boxes”: one construct, two ends.
Jobs-to-be-done (Christensen, Moesta) “The unit is the struggling moment and the forces around a switch.” “Pains are properties of a customer.” They belong to a situation.
Lean (Blank, Ries, Maurya) “Write it in an hour and expect most of it to be wrong.” “Spend a day making it consistent.”
Design research (Beyer, Holtzblatt) “Right in the abstract and wrong in the moment is wrong.” “Two lists are a sufficient record.”
Value-based pricing (Anderson, Narus) “A proposition is a quantified difference against the next-best alternative.” “The reference point is the customer's pain.”

3. Mechanics in depth

The taught sequence is: build the profile, rank, build the value map, assert the correspondences, test. Experts add four steps usually left implicit.

Step one: fix the unit before the content. The unit is a segment and a role within it, not a company. Elaan's segment holds three roles whose pain rankings differ — owner, lab manager, phlebotomist — and disagree in sign, not merely in degree. Two owners ranked six pains almost identically; a lab manager at one of their chains produced an order sharing no direction with theirs.

Step two: price the pains before relieving them. A pain not stated as a recurring cost in a currency the customer manages cannot be ranked or priced. Elaan's reference chain: eight collection centres, one processing lab, 1,80,000 samples a year, 240 referring doctors, ₹4.56 crore of revenue, a realisation near ₹253 a sample, every line from counts the chain's systems already produce.

Step three: score the gap, not the complaint. Step four: write the decision rule first, and check that it can discriminate. 4. When it applies, as testable claims

Four conditions must hold, and each is tested below against both protagonists.

One: the pains of the chosen role can be ranked by a measure the role itself would recognise. Elaan passes for owners (ρ = +0.886) and fails across roles (ρ = −0.371): two canvases, not one. Elanta fails outright: one canvas spanning the operator who buys and the driver who acts.

Two: each pain can be priced in a currency the customer manages. Elaan passes; every ledger line reduces to rupees a year from counts the chain keeps. Elanta passes for the operator in rental rupees, and for the driver only once recovered vehicle-days become rupees a month. A proposition quantified in the wrong unit is unquantified.

Three: the relief is observable within the time the decision allows. Elaan fails on its largest pain: doctor churn costs ₹13.30 lakh a year, but ninety days cannot observe annual referral behaviour, so the honest entry is zero. Elanta passes; idle days are visible in a fortnight.

Four: the party who gains is the party who must change behaviour, or a mechanism connects them. Elaan passes with a caveat — the phlebotomist bears the alert friction while the owner banks the saving. Elanta fails, and that is the whole of Chonkar's problem.

Two situations make the canvas actively misleading. In a new category there is no practice whose pains can be elicited: asking what hurts about a job nobody does yet produces fluent fiction, and the instrument is a demand test. In a compliance purchase the pain is a statutory deadline, which one importance scale understates badly: overwhelming on audit day, irrelevant after.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies. The unit is a proposition; the customer experiences a portfolio. Where Elaan's older billing module already relieves part of the reconciliation pain, Esvara can claim only the increment. Mature firms keep a pain library keyed to the customer, not the product, so two teams cannot both bank the same ₹6.20 lakh of disputed receivables. Most say they do; fewer have the library.

Two-sided situations. A reliever on one side is often a pain creator on the other: a strict turnaround guarantee relieves the referring doctor and burdens the processing lab. Expert practice is two canvases plus a cross-side ledger, written the moment you write the reliever, not at the review where the other side's churn appears.

Regulated products. A regulator has no canvas: nothing to relieve, nothing to delight. Elaan's NABL line is worth ₹1.80 lakh a year as documentation effort, but the requirement is a constraint on the solution space, not a pain to trade off. Constraints belong above the canvas, as filters on the value map.

Hardware plus software. A software reliever can be withdrawn in a release; a hardware reliever cannot. Elanta's dongle carries ₹3,400 per vehicle, so on 320 vehicles hardware alone is ₹10.88 lakh of capital against an operator gain of ₹18.51 lakh. Relievers need a cost column from the first workshop: the asymmetry between reversible and irreversible relievers sets the order of building.

AI-native products. Here the grammar breaks, because a probabilistic reliever relieves a pain only distributionally. Benedita Cardoso, Elaan's applied-research lead in Lisbon, reported the tube-and-label model on a deliberately enriched test set: 2,400 images of which 350 were mislabelled, a sensitivity of 92.0 per cent, a false-positive rate of 4.8 per cent, test-set precision of 76.7 per cent. In the field the in-scope prevalence is 1.97 per cent, not 14.6, and precision collapses.

Realised relief from a probabilistic reliever is a product of three terms, only one of which the model team controls: detection, compliance, in-scope share. This is also where accountability disappears: the model team owns detection, operations compliance, nobody scope.

6. Six nuances that separate expert from competent

The unit is a role, not a logo. The tell is a pain list in mixed registers: “re-collections cost us money” beside “I get shouted at by the consultant”. The obvious reading is that the canvas is rich; the correct one is that it is two canvases superimposed, which is what Exhibit 2 shows measured.

Relievers have a friction cost; relief is net. The tell is a deck that says eliminates while the pilot log shows a queue. Esvara's queue runs 11,694 flags a year at ninety seconds each: ₹0.70 lakh of phlebotomist time against ₹6.08 lakh of avoided re-collections, so net relief is ₹5.38 lakh and gross overstates it by 11.5 per cent of itself. Where false-positive rates are high the overstatement can exceed the relief.

Denominators drift across a discovery series. The tell is a prevalence table in which every row shares one denominator, which almost never happens in fieldwork. Elaan's reconciliation question entered at interview 15, so its base is 29 and not 43; section 8 shows what dividing by 43 would have cost.

A model's accuracy is a ceiling, not a claim. The tell is a reliever whose demo number and pilot delta differ by a factor nobody can name. The missing factors are behavioural or definitional, and an expert asks for the decomposition before the accuracy figure — the one term certain to be measured well.

Gains must land on whoever must change behaviour. The tell is a signed contract with no usage. Esadhan's recovered day is worth ₹1,000, split ₹420 to the operator who buys and ₹580 to the driver who must follow the schedule — about ₹666 a month per driver, against the ₹1,517 the drivers themselves named. A gain creator below the acting party's behaviour-change threshold is not a gain creator.

The reference point is the alternative, not the status quo. The tell is a team that can state a pain's annual cost but not what the incumbent tool already relieves of it. This is Anderson and Narus's resonating focus, and the commonest reason a canvas that survives discovery dies in a competitive deal: the relief was real and not differential.

8.2 Elanta Mobility: the gain that landed on the wrong person

Chonkar's fleet runs 320 vehicles six days a week, 313 revenue days a year, for 1,00,160 revenue vehicle-days. Cutting idle days from 11.4 to 7.0 per cent of revenue days recovers 4.4 points, or 4,407 vehicle-days. A revenue day collects ₹1,150 of fares less ₹150 of energy, leaving ₹1,000 split ₹420 of rental to the operator and ₹580 to the driver. The operator's gain is 4,407 × ₹420 = ₹18.51 lakh against 320 × ₹1,450 = ₹4.64 lakh.

Chonkar's first board pack measured idle days over calendar days: 320 × 365 = 1,16,800, giving 5,139 days and ₹21.58 lakh. The fleet does not run on Sundays, so calendar days count days on which no revenue was possible. The correction is ₹3.07 lakh, 14.2 per cent of the claim, and the ratio moves from 4.65 to 3.99 times. It does not change the decision, which turns on the other side of the split.

Drivers collect 4,407 × ₹580 = ₹25.56 lakh — more than the operator — but over 320 drivers that is ₹7,988 a year, about ₹666 a month. Elanta asked the 31 driver-partners who stayed behind after a depot meeting, volunteers from a fleet of 320, what weekly bonus would make them follow a schedule daily; 24 of the 31, or 77 per cent, named ₹300 to ₹400 a week, median ₹350, or ₹1,517 a month. The driver's share is 44 per cent of that, so behaviour did not change and the operator's ₹18.51 lakh never materialised. Diverting ₹120 of the operator's ₹420 lifts the driver to ₹700 a recovered day, but each driver recovers only 4,407 ÷ 320 = 13.77 days a year, worth ₹9,640, or ₹803 a month — still short. The arithmetic therefore forces a segment change, not a price change, and fixes the cutoff. A driver needs 26.0 recovered days at ₹700 to clear ₹1,517 a month, 8.3 points of 313 days above the 7.0 per cent floor: break-even is a 15.3 per cent baseline, so a 15 per cent cutoff fails at its own edge. Elanta set it at 16 per cent — 28.17 days, ₹19,719 a year, ₹1,643 a month — and at 18 per cent, 11 points of 313 days is 34.43 days, ₹24,101 a year, ₹2,008 a month, with the operator keeping 34.43 × ₹300 = ₹10,329 a vehicle against ₹1,450 of price, 7.1 times. Its pipeline holds 38 such operators of 268, or 14.2 per cent.

8.3 Elamba Learning: where the approach failed

Elamba Learning, in Indore, ran an exemplary-looking canvas in September 2024 for Esanket, an adaptive remedial-practice product. Its founder, Benaifer Chinwalla, had rich parent pains, vivid student gains, a teacher adoption story. The flaw was one canvas for three roles, compounded by a base error. The case of 14 November 2024 multiplied a stated willingness to pay of ₹1,180 per student per year by 42,000 students in 31 signed schools: ₹4.96 crore. The committee's standing rule — year-two revenue of at least 95 per cent of committed build spend, here ₹1.40 crore of engineering and ₹0.70 crore of content — set the gate at ₹2.00 crore; at 50 per cent conversion the case showed ₹2.48 crore and passed.

Two bases were wrong. Esanket covered grades six to nine, 18,500 of the 42,000 enrolled, or 44.0 per cent; of those, a parent survey with 1,240 responses found 61 per cent with the required home device access, leaving 11,285 eligible students. At ₹1,180 that is ₹1.33 crore, and at 50 per cent conversion ₹0.67 crore. Worse, the ₹1,180 came from a “would you pay” question: in the first paid cohort 128 of 1,120 eligible parents paid, 11.4 per cent, putting year-two revenue at 11,285 × 0.114 × ₹1,180 = ₹15.2 lakh. A project that cleared the gate by 24 per cent misses it by more than an order of magnitude.

The failure surfaced in July 2025, nine months in, with ₹0.88 crore of the ₹1.40 crore engineering budget spent. Chinwalla killed the parent-paid product and re-scoped to the one role whose pain Elamba had priced correctly and ignored: the teacher's marking load. Of the ₹0.88 crore, ₹0.26 crore of platform work was reusable, so ₹0.62 crore was written off. The teacher tool cost ₹0.40 crore and sold to the school at ₹88,000 a year; in year two it reached 127 schools and ₹1.12 crore of revenue at a 71 per cent gross margin. The same rule on a ₹0.40 crore build set the bar at ₹0.38 crore, which the ₹1.12 crore cleared nearly three times over. The recovery was not a better proposition for the same customer but the abandonment of a customer for one whose pain had been priced.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether pains and gains are two constructs or one. The canonical school keeps them separate because each prompt yields different material. Ulwick's holds that they are one construct — a desired outcome scored for importance and satisfaction — and that two boxes license double-counting: the same need as a pain and as its mirror-image gain, then summed. Nobody has measured whether two-box canvases overstate opportunity, which is what would settle it.

Whether to rank pains by money or by opportunity score. Phlebotomist retention scores 13.7, second of six, and Esvara relieves none of it; reconciliation scores 11.7, third, and delivers 39 per cent of all verified relief. The pricing school says only money supports a price. The ODI school says money projects the firm's ability to monetise rather than customer need, and under-invests in the pains a new entrant will build on. The money ranking is wrong here only if retention becomes somebody's wedge into Elaan's accounts.

Whether the canvas should be quantified at all. The lean position, steelmanned: quantification is premature precision that buys false confidence. Exhibit 7 took Elaan nine months, long enough for a segment to move, and Ash Maurya's Lean Canvas reduces the apparatus to three problems and one line, cycle time being the binding early constraint. The counter is that the ledger is what let Chemburkar defend a price. The lean position holds only if the information decays no faster than it is acquired: in fast consumer categories it plainly does, in Elaan's lab economics it plainly does not, and nobody has shown that category velocity explains the whole disagreement.

Whether a canvas should name a competitor. Anderson and Narus require a quantified difference against the next-best alternative; the canonical canvas has no slot for it, and its defenders argue that naming one early anchors the team on feature parity. Both sides are uncomfortable: canvases without a named alternative lose deals they should win, and canvases with one produce roadmaps that read like a competitor's release notes. Most experts sequence, status quo before alternative, which is a practice rather than a resolution.

The signature of mastery is an order of questions. Someone who has studied the canvas starts at the content; someone who has internalised it starts at the unit and the denominator, having learned that the wrong unit cannot be repaired by better content. The second signature is comfort with empty cells: pains with no reliever, a candid zero where ninety days could not observe an annual behaviour. The gaps are where the next experiment comes from. The third is willingness to narrow, as Chonkar's 16 per cent cutoff shows: arithmetic on both sides dictates the segment.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 27 March 2026 Chemburkar took Esvara to the committee at ₹2.40 lakh with the ledger as presented, and changed the proposition rather than the price. She cut the turnaround-time claim from the sales deck — ₹13.30 lakh of real pain against which Elaan could not evidence relief, and so could not defend at renewal. She put the ₹0.81 lakh friction column on the customer-facing page, on Brinda Castelino's argument that implementation leads find the alert queue in week three and lose trust if it was undisclosed. She flagged the reconciliation row's interval to the committee, opened a separate canvas for phlebotomist retention, and rewrote the decision rule: more labs, fewer participants each.

On 20 February 2026 Chonkar declined to scale Esadhan at ₹1,450 a vehicle. He split the canvas in two, funded a driver-facing earnings view by diverting ₹120 of the operator's ₹420 recovered rental into a daily bonus, and restricted two quarters of selling to the 38 pipeline operators at or above a 16 per cent baseline idle rate, where the driver clears the ₹1,517 threshold — ₹1,643 a month at 16 per cent, ₹2,008 at 18. Chawathe was told to make the dongle report unplugging, now the proposition's leading indicator.

Discussion questions

  1. Chemburkar booked zero relief against the ₹13.30 lakh turnaround pain because ninety days cannot observe annual referral behaviour. Was that right, or did she leave her largest claim for a competitor who will simply assert it? What ninety-day evidence would have justified a non-zero entry?
  2. Elanta’s calendar-to-revenue-day correction moved ₹3.07 lakh and changed nothing; Elaan’s one denominator moved ₹4.00 lakh and decided the product. What distinguishes a base error that matters, and can that be known before the correction?
  3. Chinwalla’s recovery abandoned the customer the canvas was built for. When is “change the customer” right, and when is it an expensive way of avoiding the harder finding — that the pain was real and the company could not relieve it?
